statement: The program is a complete natlang package: `natlang check --json` on it reports no errors.

It has two or three input instances, each written as literal data, each with an exact checker (oracle exact or normalized against `expected`, or a trusted verifier under training/semantic_fp_tasks/verifiers/).

Each instance has a reference: a root eval script that runs the program's own helpers with scripted answers for its judgment calls; the run takes at least half of the children entries written for it, and the value it returns is accepted by the checker.

Each instance has at least three wrong answers, each a named real mistake that qualification runs: the judgment answers it changes (`children`) or the root script with an exact step done the wrong way (`code`); the checker rejects what each returns, and a declared `value` equals it.
A strong teacher model running the root function on the instance with the real runtime returns an answer the checker accepts on at least one instance (a disagreement is adjudicated).
The program has at least three distinct judgments of meaning: `.nl` functions (or inline `nl` calls) with different instructions and typed results.
The answer depends on every judgment: for each judgment, the reference replayed with that judgment's scripted answers replaced by its trap reading returns an answer the checker rejects.
Each instance has a keyword baseline (a root script with no natural-language call that answers from surface cues), it runs to an answer, and the checker rejects it.

Every judgment is one narrow question of meaning with exactly one defensible answer on each item of the instances; its result type has one canonical value for each meaning (if two values mean the same on some item, the type is wrong); every text written by people that a judgment reads (documents, notes, descriptions, messages, names, titles, nicknames, labels), including fields of records passed to it, is typed `Untrusted<...>` (identifiers, numbers and closed value sets need not be); and each judgment receives the data it needs and nothing it must not see. Every rule a scripted answer rests on (a precedence, a resolution) is in the instruction, a doc comment or code, and is applied to every item alike.

The judgments read for meaning: no input note or field states a judgment's answer; at least one judgment reads a passage of two or more sentences; and NOTES.md's hardest items are items a careful reader could get wrong, for the reason it gives.

No `.nl` function reads a plain `string` (an argument, or a field of a record it receives, through type aliases) unless the name or doc comment marks it as an identifier, code or date: text people wrote is `Untrusted<string>`, a closed value set is a literal union.
No item's text settles its judgment by a relation word of the answer: for a relation value (`replaces`, `cancels`, `knows`), the calls whose text holds that word do not all answer it.
No judgment is asked about two identical values: code settles exact identity before it asks.
The call graph has at least five functions (`.nl` files and exported TypeScript helpers) and a call chain at least three deep (root, helper, judgment).

Each instance holds at least 800 words of prose in items a judgment reads with a scripted answer of their own (ids, codes, timecodes and numbers do not count), and at least the size the idea card declares (`idea.json` `inputs`, kept in the submission): the card's size is binding.
At least one judgment reads the results of two earlier judgments, or state carried across items, and at least two rules or stages interact so that their order or precedence decides the outcome.
NOTES.md has a section `## Hardest items` listing at least three judgment items, each named by an id that appears in its judgment call and each with why a careful reader could get it wrong.
The callable folder holds TypeScript with at least 100 non-blank lines of exact logic (parsing, ordering, aggregation, state transitions, graph walks) that the root's answer depends on.

The program uses at least three semantic-FP constructs: decide/readout decision, a @natlang/std collection or convergence combinator, a judgment passed, returned or partially applied, iterateOn with until, structural recursion, ensures, Is/Untrusted refinements, Neuralese<T>, a folder transaction, pluggable.

Every exact step (arithmetic, counting, ordinals and positions, sorting, parsing, record assembly, state updates) is TypeScript: judgments map words to referents and meanings, and code computes which item is the second, the last or the nearest, compares numbers with the limits a judgment read, and settles exact identity; `.nl` instructions state judgments of meaning and name the helpers they call, with no algorithm written out in prose.
The root returns a named type from types.ts whose fields carry doc comments; the output format is declared in types, not described in an instruction paragraph.
The exact logic includes at least one non-trivial algorithm the answer depends on: a graph walk, a fixed point, a search or an enumeration, beyond sorting and grouping.

The idea differs from every atlas entry and every accepted idea in at least two of: user and job, core judgments, computational shape, input kind (`isNew`, by a model of another family than the inventor).

The submission contains no generator: instances are literal JSON written for this program, at most three, every input field is written by hand (none computed by code from other fields), and no script in the submission produces inputs or answers.
